newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU officials head west for U.S. air talks opener.
newsitem.headline: EU officials head west for U.S. air talks opener.

text.p: Officials from the European Commission, most of the 15 EU member states and representatives from Europe's airlines will converge on Washington next week for getting-to-know-you open skies talks with U.S. counterparts.
"We view them as preliminary discussions and not an inauguration of negotiations," Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said of the talks at a news conference on Thursday.

"First of all there is a task of explanation to be conducted, simply because of the divergences between the regulatory, legal and commercial systems on both sides of the Atlantic. Secondly there's the small matter of the (U.S.) presidential elections in a couple of weeks' time," he said.

A U.S. official confirmed the generally downbeat view of the meeting, the first official face-to-face contact between the sides since EU transport ministers gave Kinnock the go-ahead for his part-mandate in June.
He said the United States would be "in listening mode only".
"The first meeting will be largely procedural. We are interested to hear what the Commission's mandate is, how far it can go. We have not put anything on the table." the official told Reuters.

Kinnock's mandate is to begin talks on so-called soft rights -- things like slot allocation, ground-handling rules, competition policy, code sharing and computer reservation systems -- leaving more touchy issues such as airline ownership rules and traffic rights for later sessions and then only once EU member states allow him.
"You cannot get very far on the issues which are of most interest to the Commission and member states without talking about the underlying issue of traffic rights," the official said.
First talks are intended to look at things like whether to break negotiations into sub-groups on single issues and what should be the schedule for meetings over the coming months.

"Prospects depend to a large extent how much the member states are prepared to cede to the Commission. It can discuss traffic rights but only where they are related to other subjects. They obviously cannot put rights on the table and without that, it's not a negotiation," the official said.
One of the things at the back of officials' minds will be ongoing bilateral talks between the United States and Britain.
"We expect to have something in place, which in our view will be a full open skies arrangement, by April next year, probably earlier," the official said.

He added that such a deal, along with those negotiated between the United States and Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden, would sew up about two thirds of the north Atlantic market.

Then comes France, whose flag carrier Air France recently signed letters of intent to cooperate with U.S. carriers Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines, which has had on-off open skies talks with Washington for a while.
"For anything short of open skies it would be far preferable for us to stick to the current agreement," the official said of planned fresh talks with Paris.
"I think that the French government may now find it more beneficial to have an open skies agreement," he said.

Then there is Spain, where government indications are that state-owned carrier Iberia is headed for privatisation, something the official sees as presaging an alliance with one of the U.S. companies and eventual bilateral talks on traffic rights from Spain to the U.S. and Latin America.

"It's hard to know what would be left if we make significant progress with France or Spain. It may well be that we are in a race with the Commission to nail down as many of these things before having to discuss (U.S.) cabotage and ownership rights.
"I don't think we will have much interest in changing our ownership rules until we discuss traffic rights and even then, I don't know how keen we would be to change those rules," he said.

Council Regulation 2407/92 allows U.S. interests to take up to 49 percent of the shares of a Community carrier, provided that control remains in Community hands. In April 1995, when the Commission adopted its draft mandate, U.S. law limited foreign ownership to 25 percent of an airline's voting stock, again provided that control remained in U.S. hands.

Kinnock disagreed that talks would be rendered pointless by the ongoing and future bilateral talks between EU member states and the U.S. or that such deals would leave little to excite Washington in what remained.
"Ultimately there's got to be some kind of parity of legal and commercial standards between the two sides," he told Reuters after Thursday's news conference.
"Our market will grow and so it's commercially attractive. To have full and effective access to that market there's an entry fee," he said.

"It's not too late in all these developments, it's early days. It's early days for most of the European bilateral partnerships because the access which some of the airlines have to the USA is, if I were to say marginal it would be an exaggeration, whereas the access the other way is significant. That's a balance which ultimately is unsustainable," he said.
